title: Back to the Shower
question: Why did we oscillate, and how close to the edge are we?

blocks.text: I put our drone PID on the shower. It swung hot, cold, hot… exactly like Mika in Chapter 0. The drone never did that!
The drone has no big delay. The shower has 2.5 seconds of pipe. Let's finally work out what a delay *does*.

First, a confession about Chapter 0's "normal hand". It turned the knob at a **speed** proportional to how wrong the water felt: knob speed $= k\cdot\err{e}$, with $k = 0.8\,\%$ of the knob per second per °C. A speed proportional to the error means the knob *position* is the pile of past error. That's an **I controller**, with $K_i = k$.
For calculations the knob runs from 0 to 1, so 0.8% of its range is 0.008 knob units. The loop formula below uses 0.008; the sliders display 0.8%. Keep the units with the number.
Wait, so in Chapter 0 I was a PID controller? Well, an I controller. An over-eager one.

sections.title: Delay is a lag in the wiggle

blocks.text: I still think a delay just makes everything *slower*. It shouldn't be able to make anything unstable.

Let's isolate the pipe's **pure delay** first. Imagine a sine wave at the pipe's input travelling to the showerhead with no smoothing: the output has the same shape, 2.5 s late. How late is that, *compared with one wiggle*?

The pipe delay stays at 2.5 s, but its **phase lag** depends on how fast the wave wiggles. Call the lag $\phi$. If one wiggle takes $T$ seconds, its angular speed is $\omega=2\pi/T$ radians per second. A positive lag here means the output trails the input; on a phase plot, that appears as a negative angle. With a delay of $L$ seconds, we can express the same lag in degrees or radians:

For a slow 30-second wiggle, 2.5 s is only 30°: a small shift. For a 5-second wiggle it is 180°: in this pure-delay model, each output crest lines up with an input trough. The shower's thermal response also smooths fast wiggles; we'll add that next.
This is the spinning arrow from Chapter 5: a delay of $L$ rotates the arrow $e^{i\omega t}$ backwards by the angle $\omega L$. That's why the transfer function of a pure delay is $e^{-Ls}$.

sections.title: Measuring the shower one wiggle at a time

blocks.text: Now add the shower's thermal response to the pipe delay. Changes in water temperature take time to settle, so the full shower both delays and smooths knob changes. Here's the plan: wiggle the knob at one speed, wait for a steady rhythm, and measure two numbers:

items: **Gain:** how big the temperature wiggle is, compared with the wiggle in the water mix we asked for.
**Phase:** how far behind it is, as an angle.

blocks.text: Each measurement drops a dot on two plots. Measure at least five speeds, slow and fast.

The shower's thermal lag shrinks fast wiggles, while the pipe keeps adding phase lag. These gain and phase curves against wiggle speed form a **Bode plot**. Here the input is the **temperature of the mixed water**, so slow wiggles have gain 1. If we used knob fraction as input, the gain would be 45 times larger. For this temperature-to-temperature plot, set $s=i\omega$ in the normalized shower response:

One honest assist: a single measurement can't tell a lag of 90° from 450° (the waves look the same). We count whole extra cycles by following the curve from slow to fast, like tracking one crest through the pipe.
Now close the loop: hand → knob → pipe → skin → hand. Follow a wiggle all the way around. For the Chapter 0 hand, the trip around the loop is

Feedback subtracts (error = target − temperature), which flips the wave once. If the trip around the loop *also* delays it by exactly 180°, the two flips cancel, and every correction arrives **perfectly in step** with the swing, like pushing a playground swing at just the right moment. If the loop also doesn't shrink the wave (gain ≥ 1), the swing grows by itself.

For this simple shower loop, the phase falls through −180° at one relevant wiggle speed. Find that speed on the phase plot, then read the loop gain at the same speed on the gain plot. Is it below or above 1?

For example, near 0.457 rad/s the accumulating hand lags by 90°, mixing adds about 25°, and the pipe adds about 65°: together, 180°. The normal hand returns a swing only about 0.72 times as large. It could be about 1 ÷ 0.72 ≈ 1.4 times stronger before reaching the edge.

items.def: How many times you could multiply the controller's gain before the loop gain reaches 1 at the −180° speed. Below 1 = over the cliff.
At the speed where the loop gain is exactly 1, how much *extra* lag it would take to reach −180°. More is safer; 45°–60° is a common target.

blocks.text: For our shower, the phase of $L$ hits −180° at $\omega \approx 0.457$ rad/s, a wiggle period of about **13.8 s**. The normal hand ($k = 0.008$) has a gain margin of only about **1.4**, and a phase margin of about 22°. Close to the edge! The harder hand doubles the gain: 1.4 ÷ 2 = 0.7, **over the cliff**. That's exactly why it never settled.

blocks.q: Suppose the pipe were twice as long (a 5 s delay). What happens to the largest hand gain that's still stable?

options.text: It goes **up**: you can react harder, because you have more time
options.why: More time to react sounds nice, but you're reacting to *older* news. The lag grows at every speed.

options.text: It goes **down**: you must react more gently
options.why: The phase hits −180° at a slower wiggle, and at slow speeds the hand's pile ($k/s$) is big. The loop gain there is larger, so $k$ must shrink: from about 1.12 to 0.60 %/(°C·s).

options.text: It stays the same: delay changes timing, not gain
options.why: A delay doesn't change the size of a wave, true, but it changes *which* speed reaches −180°, and the gain is different there.

blocks.text: Okay, I take it back. A delay doesn't just make things slower: it eats phase margin, and phase margin is the only thing between you and an oscillation.
Here's your own run from Chapter 0. If your swings were near the edge, their period should be close to what the loop predicts. There's a twist: people are not all the same kind of controller.

A **speed hand** (turn the knob while it feels wrong) is an I controller: its edge is at 13.8 s swings. A **position hand** ("it's too hot, put the knob *here*") acts like a P controller: $L(s) = 45K\,e^{-2.5s}/(s+1)$, whose phase hits −180° at $\omega \approx 0.95$ rad/s, **6.6 s** swings, for any $K$ above about 0.031 knob per °C. Most people are a mix. (The normal robot hand swings a bit slower than 13.8 s, about 15.5 s, because it sits just inside the edge; the harder hand's swings, about 11.6 s, are squashed by the knob hitting its ends.)

Now let’s beat our own hands. The robot uses PI: **P reacts to the current temperature error**, and **I remembers accumulated error**. Together they let the knob respond promptly while I finds the right lasting setting. Compared with I alone, P can add phase lead. Aim for a **phase margin above 45°** and **10 seconds in the comfort band starting within 12 s**.

The robot code writes PI as a knob **speed**: I keeps moving the knob while error remains, and P responds to a *change* in error. At startup, P also gives the knob an immediate move based on the current error. This matches the position rule, except when the knob reaches an end stop.
Easy. I'll use big gains, like on the drone: fast and snappy.
…it swings exactly like we did. Big gains pushed the −180° speed past the point where the loop gain is 1. No phase margin at all.
The drone could take big gains because it had almost no lag. Here, **robust** means gentle: leave margin for the delay. Try about $K_p \approx 1$ and $K_i \approx 0.6$.

These slider numbers are percentages of the full knob range: P ≈ 1% per °C of current error, and I ≈ 0.6% per °C-second of accumulated error. The loop equations use knob fractions, so divide the displayed numbers by 100.

A well-margined PI gets comfortable in about 9.4 seconds, without repeated large swings. That beats the normal hand (which spent most of a minute swinging before it calmed down) and most humans. It can't beat physics, though: nothing can react to water that hasn't arrived yet. Engineers do have a trick for long delays, a **Smith predictor**, which runs a little simulation of the pipe inside the controller. That's a story for another notebook.

Robustness is the real lesson. Your model of the shower is never perfect: the pipe might be longer, the heater weaker. Margins are the insurance that your controller still works when the world isn't quite what you assumed.

items: A delay $L$ lags a wiggle by $\omega L$: nothing for slow wiggles, a lot for fast ones.
Feeding in sine waves and measuring gain and phase gives the **frequency response**; plotted, it's a **Bode plot**, and it's just $G(i\omega)$.
For this simple shower loop, self-sustained oscillation begins when the loop reaches −180° phase with gain 1; larger gain makes the swings grow until limits intervene.
**Gain and phase margin** measure the distance to that cliff. Longer delay means less margin, so you need gentler control.
Our Chapter 0 swings were a controller (us) with too little margin.

items.q: A 2 s delay, and a wiggle with an 8 s period. How much phase lag does the delay add?

options.why: 2 s is a quarter of 8 s, and a quarter of 360° is 90°.
That would be a delay of 1 s. 2 s is a quarter of the period, not an eighth.
That would need a delay of half the period, 4 s.

items.q: At the speed where the loop's phase is −180°, the loop gain is 0.5. What is the gain margin?

options.why: You could double the gain before the loop gain at −180° reaches 1.
That's the loop gain itself. The margin is how far it is to 1: 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.
Gain margin is a factor, not an angle. The angle version is the phase margin.

items.q: Why does a longer pipe force a gentler controller?

options.text: The extra lag reaches −180° at a slower wiggle, where the loop gain is bigger, so the gain must come down
options.why: Right. For an integrating hand, slow wiggles get the biggest boost, so the cliff moves closer.

options.text: The water gets colder in a longer pipe
options.why: We assumed no heat loss. The effect is purely about timing.

options.text: It doesn't: you can react harder since you have more time
options.why: You don't have more time. You have older information. That's the trap from Chapter 0.

items.q: The normal hand has a gain margin of about 1.4. What happens if you react 1.5 times harder?

options.text: The swings grow instead of dying out
options.why: 1.5 is more than the 1.4 margin, so the loop gain at −180° goes past 1: over the cliff.
More gain would only help if there were plenty of margin. With 1.4, there isn't.
Gain is exactly what the gain margin measures, so it definitely matters.

blocks.text: We have every tool now: feedback, PID, poles, margins. Time for the real test: wind, a package drop, and a noisy sensor. **Can you keep the drone at 2 m?**
